passage:
Community centre note, written by Kishore.
Parveen has come to our Thursday tea evenings for two years. When the subject of the blocked drain outside the lane came up, she said, "Forget it. They've ignored it for five years. Nothing changes." Others nodded, and the room went quiet.
I did not argue. I asked if she would sign one page with twenty other names, asking for a written reply. She said no at first, then took the pen. We sent it that week. The ward office replied within days and cleared part of the drain. Parveen said, "Only part." But she came the following Thursday and brought the second page for the neighbours to sign.

qa.q: How long has Parveen been coming to the Thursday tea evenings?
qa.a: Parveen has come for two years.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when she said 'Forget it. Nothing changes'?
qa.a: Parveen felt weary and discouraged after years of being ignored, though the note only records what she said.

qa.q: What did Kishore do that helped move Parveen from cynicism to a small action?
qa.a: Kishore did not argue but asked her to sign one shared page asking for a written reply, and sent it the same week.

qa.q: How might Kishore see Parveen's words 'Only part'?
qa.a: Kishore probably saw them as Parveen's usual caution rather than a refusal, since the note records that she came back the next Thursday with the second page.

grounding: A citizen who has seen many delays decides that nothing can change, and a small shared complaint changes how the office behaves.

passage:
Sunday. Baljeet Uncle used to be the loudest complainer on our lane. Today I asked about the streetlight, and he just waved a hand. "Ten years of complaints. It's the same file in the same drawer." He said it flatly and went back to his crossword.
I don't blame him. He has stood in so many queues. But the pole has been dark for a month, and the lane is bad at night.
So tonight I wrote a short, polite complaint with the pole number and asked six neighbours to sign it. Baljeet Uncle read it, sighed, and signed last, muttering that nothing will change. I'll send it tomorrow and note the date.
Divyansh

qa.q: What did Baljeet Uncle say about ten years of complaints?
qa.a: He said it was the same file in the same drawer.

qa.q: What is Divyansh feeling about Baljeet Uncle's tiredness?
qa.a: Divyansh feels understanding and a little sad, saying Divyansh does not blame him for standing in so many queues.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do next that could shift the situation?
qa.a: Divyansh wrote a short polite complaint with the pole number, gathered six neighbour signatures and plans to send it and note the date.

qa.q: How does Baljeet Uncle seem to see complaints now?
qa.a: He thinks nothing will change after ten years, but he still read the page and signed last, so he has not quite given up.

grounding: A citizen who has seen many delays decides nothing can change and stops trying, while a small shared complaint is still made.

passage:
In their small town of Karad, the streetlight at the bus stop had been broken for a year. Zubin, twenty-five, had given up. "Nothing works here," he told anyone who asked. "Why waste breath?"
His neighbour Ishita didn't give up. Every Monday, she walked to the municipal office and filed the same complaint. Zubin watched her go and shook his head.
In the third month, she came to his door with a paper. "Sign this. Twenty-three of us. The girls from the college walk past that stop at night."
Zubin sighed and signed, mostly to be polite.
Four weeks later, he came home from work to find the bus stop bright. Ishita was standing under it, grinning.
Zubin stood beside her for a moment. "I thought you were wasting your time," he admitted.
"Everyone did," she said. "Next week: the drain."

qa.q: How many people signed Ishita's paper?
qa.a: Twenty-three of them signed.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when he watched Ishita go every Monday?
qa.a: Zubin felt tired, hopeless and cynical, sure that her complaints were a waste of time.

qa.q: What does Ishita's success teach?
qa.a: Small, steady acts and shared complaints can change how offices behave over time, even after a year of neglect.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel standing under the working light?
qa.a: Ishita probably feels proud and happy, rewarded after months of persistence.

grounding: In a small town, a weary citizen who believes nothing can change watches a neighbour's persistent, shared complaints succeed.

subtopic: Dealing with bureaucracy and corruption pressure
passage:
In Lagos, the pothole at the corner of Emeka's street had been there so long that children named it "the Lake." Emeka, twenty-six, had written to the local council once, years ago, and heard nothing. Now he just drove around it and said, "This is Nigeria. Nothing changes."
His neighbour Vera, a nurse, had different ideas. She set up a street group chat, collected photos from twenty households, and sent a joint letter every two weeks to the council, copying a local radio station.
Emeka rolled his eyes but added his photo.
Three months later, the radio station read the letter on air. The next week, a council truck arrived with gravel and tar.
Emeka stood on the new surface, stamping his foot. Vera laughed. "Still think nothing changes?"
"Something changed," he admitted. "Next letter, I'll write it."

qa.q: What did the children name the pothole?
qa.a: The children named it "the Lake."

qa.q: What was Emeka feeling when he said "Nothing changes"?
qa.a: Emeka felt tired, hopeless and cynical after writing once years ago and hearing nothing.

qa.q: What did Vera do that changed the outcome?
qa.a: She gathered photos from many households, sent regular joint letters and copied a radio station, turning single complaints into shared pressure.

qa.q: How might Vera feel when Emeka offers to write the next letter?
qa.a: Vera would likely feel pleased and encouraged that his cynicism has softened into action.

grounding: Outside India, a weary citizen who believes nothing can change sees a neighbour's shared complaints succeed, and joins in.

passage: In the waiting hall of the municipal ward office, Chetan sat with his water complaint and token 47. Beside him, Yash, a man from his colony, laughed without humour. "Fourth time I'm here about the same leak. Nothing changes in this country. I've stopped even filing. Today I only came to pay the bill." Chetan felt the same tiredness creep up his own spine. Then he noticed a notice on the wall: "Complaints from five or more households on one street will be treated as a group case." He turned to Yash. "How many houses on our lane have the leak?" Yash shrugged. "Six? Seven?" "Then let's file one together. Seven names." Yash hesitated, then took the pen. Three weeks later a crew dug up the lane. Yash stood at his gate watching, arms folded, almost smiling.

qa.q: What token number did Chetan have?
qa.a: Chetan had token 47.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling as Yash spoke?
qa.a: Chetan felt the same weary cynicism creeping in, tempted to give up too.

qa.q: Which small act helped more than giving up?
qa.a: Noticing the group-case rule and filing one complaint together for seven households, which got the office to act.

qa.q: Why might Yash have stopped filing complaints?
qa.a: After four visits about the same leak, Yash felt tired and defeated, and cynicism seemed safer than hoping again.

grounding: It illustrates a citizen worn down into cynicism by repeated delays, and how a shared complaint shows that small honest acts can still change how an office behaves.
